blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 16 (Lab Safety and Practical Skills (running header: Identifying Hazards and Designing Safe Experiments)), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is a chemistry laboratory? Write eight general instructions that a student must follow while working in it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A chemistry laboratory is a chemist workshop: a place where a student is trained to observe the physical and chemical characteristics of substances by following definite procedures. Before starting, the student should become familiar with the layout of the laboratory and the fittings on the laboratory table and the side shelves.

General instructions:
1. Conduct yourself in a responsible manner at all times.
2. Do not work alone; perform experiments in the presence of the lab instructor and other laboratory staff.
3. Always wear a lab coat and safety goggles; girls must tie up their scarves and hair.
4. Determine the potential hazards of any equipment or experiment before beginning, and observe proper safety precautions.
5. No crowding; stick to your work place at a safe distance from others.
6. Do not bring food into the lab; never taste or smell any compound or gas.
7. Report any accident or breakage of glassware to the incharge immediately; seek the instructor's help if you cannot handle an instrument.
8. Do not pour chemicals down the drains or use the sewer for chemical waste; follow the warning signs displayed in the lab.

book_ref.quote: Students are expected to conduct themselves in a responsible manner at all times in the lab.

blocks.prompt: 2 Classify laboratory hazards. Explain how a worker can protect himself from physical and chemical hazards. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Most laboratory hazards fall into three categories: physical, chemical and biological hazards.

Physical hazards: the most common are slips and falls when working on a wet floor. A worker must take all precautions to avoid accidents such as slipping, pulling and falling. While handling broken glassware he should wear cut-resistant gloves to prevent cuts, abrasions and skin damage, and the laboratory staff must dispose of broken glassware in a special container to prevent injury.

Chemical hazards: the hazards of chemicals are shown by hazard pictograms (Figure 16.2). A laboratory worker must use chemicals according to the standard procedures, keeping in view the particular hazards and the precautions required for their safe use.

Biological hazards (third category): the most common are allergens, infectious diseases transferred from animals to humans, and viral diseases.

book_ref.quote: Most hazards which we might face while working in the laboratory fall into three categories

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the waste disposal system for chemicals in a laboratory. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chemical waste cannot be disposed of in bins or the sewer system. Most chemical wastes must be disposed of according to the rules and regulations of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA):
1. Store chemical wastes in proper containers.
2. Label the containers with the types of wastes, the date of the waste and the place of origin.
3. Transfer the containers to the allocated site, where the wastes are appropriately treated and disposed of.
4. Chemical treatment of the wastes involves neutralization, precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation or reduction.

In the laboratory itself, chemicals must not be poured down the drains and the sewer must not be used for chemical waste disposal.

book_ref.quote: Label the chemical waste containers with the types of wastes

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the first aid treatment for (i) minor and serious cuts and (ii) four kinds of eye injuries in the laboratory. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Every laboratory must have a first aid box.

(i) Cuts
Minor cuts: remove the glass piece, if any, and apply a little methylated spirit or tincture iodine with a piece of cotton; both act as disinfectant.
Serious cuts: apply pressure on the cut for about 10 minutes to stop bleeding, and consult a doctor.

(ii) Eye injuries
Acid in the eye: wash thoroughly with water and then with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution.
Alkali in the eye: wash with water followed by 1% boric acid solution.
Foreign particle in the eye: do not rub the eyes; remove the particle carefully with a soft handkerchief, then wash with water.
Soreness in the eye: put a drop of olive oil in the eyes and keep them closed for some time.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the first aid treatment for burns caused by dry heat, acids, alkalis and bromine. Why are acid and alkali burns treated differently? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Burns with dry heat (flame, hot object): apply burnol or mustard oil.
2. Acid burns: wash freely with ice cold water, then with a saturated solution of sodium bicarbonate, and again with water.
3. Alkali burns: wash freely with water, then with 1% acetic acid solution and again with water; dry the skin and apply burnol.
4. Bromine burns: wash fully with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin; wipe off the glycerin after some time and apply burnol.

Reason for the difference: an acid burn is neutralised with a weak base (sodium bicarbonate), and an alkali burn with a weak acid (acetic acid).

book_ref.quote: Burns with dry heat (flame, hot object)

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the first aid for swallowed poisons (four cases) and the methods of dealing with four kinds of fire in the laboratory. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Poisons
1. Poison swallowed: spit immediately and wash the mouth with water repeatedly.
2. Acid swallowed: drink a lot of water, or lime water, or milk of magnesia.
3. Caustic alkali swallowed: drink a lot of water and a glass of lemon or orange juice.
4. Salt of a heavy metal swallowed: take milk or the white part of an egg.

Fire
1. Clothes catch fire: do not run; wrap with a blanket or dry cotton cloth and lie down on the floor.
2. Beaker of inflammable liquid catches fire: cover it with a duster or damp cloth; this cuts off the supply of oxygen.
3. Spirit or oil catches fire: throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate; do not throw water, it will simply spread the fire.
4. Electric parts catch fire: switch off the electric supply immediately and throw sand; do not use water.

book_ref.quote: Throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate.

blocks.prompt: 7 What is volumetric analysis? Define indicator and end point. Describe how phenolphthalein is prepared and used, and why its end-point colour fades. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Volumetric analysis is used to find the concentrations of solutions by a technique called titration. In titration a solution of unknown concentration is combined slowly and carefully with a known volume of a standard solution until a colour change shows the completion of the reaction. Either solution can be taken in the burette, with the other in a conical (titration) flask.

Indicator: the substance which indicates the completion of the reaction by a change in its colour.
End point: the moment at which the indicator changes colour.

Phenolphthalein: prepared by adding one gram of the indicator to 500 cm³ of 50% ethanol. Only one to two drops are used in 10 cm³ of the solution to be titrated. Its colour changes from pink to colourless as the pH decreases.

Fading: the light pink colour that marks the end point tends to fade gradually because atmospheric carbon dioxide slowly dissolves in the solution and interferes.

book_ref.quote: until a colour change shows the completion of the reaction

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the procedure for titrating a given NaOH solution against standard HCl solution using phenolphthalein. Give the chemical equation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Materials: burette, pipette, funnel, conical flask, HCl solution, NaOH solution, phenolphthalein.
Equation: NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Procedure:
1. Rinse the pipette with distilled water and then with the NaOH solution; rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.
2. Pipette out 10 cm³ of NaOH into the conical flask and add one to two drops of phenolphthalein; the solution turns pink.
3. Rinse the burette with distilled water and then with the HCl solution; fix it upright on a clamp stand, fill it with HCl using a funnel, and remove the funnel.
4. Run a little acid into a beaker through the tap to remove any air bubble in the nozzle.
5. Note the initial reading using an anti-parallax card or white paper.
6. Place the flask on a white paper under the burette; check that the burette does not leak.
7. Add acid drop wise, swirling the flask for thorough mixing, until the pink colour just disappears (colourless). This is the end point.
8. Note the final reading; final − initial = volume of acid used.
9. After a rough titration, repeat to get at least three concordant readings agreeing within 0.1 cm³.

book_ref.quote: Pipette out 10 cm³ of NaOH solution into a conical flask.

blocks.prompt: 9 10.0 cm³ of NaOH solution is titrated with 0.10 M HCl using phenolphthalein. The initial burette reading is 0.50 cm³ and the final reading is 12.80 cm³. Find the molarity of the NaOH solution. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the volume of acid from the burette readings, then use M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ with n₁ = n₂ = 1.

book_ref.quote: Find out the molarity of NaOH solution by using the following molarity equation:

steps: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so n₁ (acid) = 1 and n₂ (base) = 1.
V₁ (acid) = final − initial = 12.80 − 0.50 = 12.30 cm³; M₁ = 0.10 M; V₂ = 10.0 cm³.

blocks.prompt: 10 In the titration of 10 cm³ NaOH with 0.080 M HCl, the burette readings (initial, final in cm³) were: rough 0.00, 13.00; titration 1: 0.20, 12.60; titration 2: 12.60, 25.10; titration 3: 0.50, 12.95. Find the concordant volume of HCl and the molarity of the NaOH. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find each volume as final − initial, average the three concordant volumes (within 0.1 cm³), and leave out the rough reading.

book_ref.quote: Volume of HCl solution used = ________ cm³

steps: 12.40, 12.50 and 12.45 agree within 0.1 cm³ (concordant); the rough value is not used.
blocks.final_answer: Concordant volume of HCl = 12.45 cm³; molarity of NaOH = 0.0996 M (about 0.10 M)

blocks.prompt: 11 What volume of 0.12 M HCl will be needed to neutralise 10 cm³ of 0.15 M NaOH solution? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rearrange the molarity equation for V₁; the 1:1 equation gives n₁ = n₂ = 1.

book_ref.quote: V₂ = Volume of base solution used

steps: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so n₁ = n₂ = 1.

blocks.prompt: 12 10 cm³ of NaOH solution is neutralised by 12.0 cm³ of 0.050 M H₂SO₄. The balanced equation is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Find the molarity of the NaOH solution. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Take n₁ and n₂ from the given balanced equation (1 for the acid, 2 for the base) and use the molarity equation.

book_ref.quote: n₂ = No. of moles of the base in the balanced chemical equation

steps: M₁ = 0.050 M, V₁ = 12.0 cm³, V₂ = 10 cm³.

blocks.prompt: 13 How are chloride, bromide and iodide ions identified in a salt? Give the observations and equations, and explain why dilute HNO₃ is added. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Experiment (same for all three): take 2 g of the solid sample, dissolve it in 5 cm³ of distilled water, acidify with a few drops of dilute HNO₃, and finally add about 5 cm³ of aqueous AgNO₃.

Reason for HNO₃: dilute nitric acid is added to prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions along with the halide ions.

book_ref.quote: Reactions involved in the above tests

rows: Thick white precipitate which dissolves in aqueous NH₃

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the test for the nitrate radical. Explain why it is a redox reaction and identify the role of aluminium. Give the balanced equation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Experiment: dissolve 2 g of the solid sample in 5 cm³ of distilled water in a clean test tube, add 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution, and finally add 3 g of powdered aluminium metal.

Observation: a characteristic smell of NH₃ gas is felt near the mouth of the test tube; the gas turns red litmus paper blue. Inference: NO₃¹⁻ ions are indicated.

Explanation: aluminium metal reduces nitrate ions (via ammonium ions, which react with aqueous NaOH) to ammonia gas. It is a redox reaction: aluminium is the reducing agent and is itself oxidised to [Al(OH)₄]¹⁻, while nitrate is reduced to NH₃. No cell or electrolysis is involved, so aluminium is not a cathode.

Balanced equation:
3NO₃¹⁻(aq) + 8Al(s) + 5OH⁻(aq) + 18H₂O(l) → 3NH₃(g) + 8[Al(OH)₄]¹⁻(aq)

book_ref.quote: The reduction of NO₃¹⁻ with aluminium metal is a redox reaction

blocks.prompt: 15 Describe the tests for the ammonium (NH₄¹⁺) and calcium (Ca²⁺) radicals with observations and equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ammonium radical: dissolve 4 g of the sample in 10 cm³ of distilled water, add NaOH solution and heat gently. Ammonia gas is evolved with a distinct smell and turns moist red litmus blue: NH₄¹⁺ ions are indicated.
NH₄¹⁺(aq) + OH¹⁻(aq) → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)

Calcium radical: dissolve 4 g of the solid sample in 10 cm³ of distilled water and make two parts.
(i) To one part add NaOH solution: a white precipitate forms which does not dissolve in excess NaOH: Ca²⁺ indicated.
(ii) To the second part add aqueous ammonia: only a slight turbidity appears or no precipitate forms: Ca²⁺ indicated.
Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Ca(OH)₂(s) (white ppt)

book_ref.quote: Take 4 g of sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ distilled water.

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the identification of the Cr³⁺ and Fe²⁺ radicals with NaOH solution and aqueous ammonia. Write the equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
For each ion, dissolve 4 g of the sample in 10 cm³ of distilled water and divide into two portions.

Chromium (Cr³⁺)
NaOH: a green precipitate appears which turns into a green solution when excess NaOH is added.
Aqueous ammonia: a green precipitate appears which is insoluble in excess ammonia.
Cr³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Cr(OH)₃(s) (green ppt)

Iron(II) (Fe²⁺)
NaOH: a green precipitate forms which turns into an orange brown precipitate after some time.
Aqueous ammonia: a white gelatinous precipitate of Fe(OH)₂ forms which quickly oxidizes to the red brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃.
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂ (green ppt)

book_ref.quote: Add 4 g sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ distilled water.

blocks.prompt: 17 Tabulate the behaviour of Al³⁺, Ca²⁺, Cr³⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺ ions with NaOH solution and with aqueous ammonia. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: In each test the salt is dissolved in distilled water and the solution is divided into two parts: NaOH solution is added to one part and aqueous ammonia to the other. Each cation forms its hydroxide precipitate, e.g. Al³⁺ + 3OH¹⁻ → Al(OH)₃(s); the colour and its behaviour in excess reagent identify the ion.

book_ref.quote: Divide this solution into two parts for further tests.

Only slight turbidity or no precipitate
Green precipitate, green solution in excess NaOH
Green precipitate, insoluble in excess ammonia
